lead: A catalogue lists dozens of bearings that share the same bore, so the designer needs one number that says which of them can do the job. That number is the required basic dynamic load rating C<sub>req</sub>. You find the equivalent load from the radial and axial forces, convert the life wanted in hours into million revolutions, and compute C<sub>req</sub>. Then you pick the smallest bearing whose catalogue rating C is at least C<sub>req</sub>, and you check static safety and the limiting speed. Pumps, fans, gearboxes, electric motors and machine tool spindles are all chosen this way.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.6 for C, P and the L10 life equation, and Chapter 5.2 for the rolling bearing types.

sections.h3: Selection means turning load and life into one number

blocks.text: A rolling bearing is not designed from a blank page; it is chosen from a catalogue. For each bearing the catalogue gives a basic dynamic load rating C: the steady load, in newtons, that would give a rating life of one million revolutions. The machine gives you a load and a life in hours. Selection is the step that turns those two into a single number you can compare with the catalogue.
The life equation of Chapter 5.6 links C, P and life. Inverting it gives the rating you must ask the catalogue for.

blocks.where: C<sub>req</sub> is the required basic dynamic load rating in N; P is the equivalent dynamic load in N; L₁₀ is the rating life in million revolutions; p = 3 for ball bearings and 10/3 for roller bearings.

blocks.text: The life hidden inside C is counted in million revolutions, so the hours must be converted before they enter the formula.

blocks.where: n is the speed in rev/min; L<sub>10h</sub> is the required life in hours; 60 changes rev/min into rev per hour and 10⁶ changes revolutions into millions.

blocks.text: Choose the smallest bearing in the size range whose C is at least C<sub>req</sub>. A larger C costs more, weighs more and needs a bigger housing, so an oversized bearing is wasted money. The rating is not the only test, though: the static rating and the limiting speed are checked as well.

Bearings are rated for one kind of load: pure radial, steady, applied through the centre. A real bearing carries a radial load F<sub>r</sub> and often an axial load F<sub>a</sub>. P is the single radial load that would wear the bearing out in the same number of revolutions as the real combination.

blocks.where: F<sub>r</sub> and F<sub>a</sub> are the radial and axial loads in N; X is the radial factor and Y the axial factor, read from the table for that bearing type.

blocks.text: For a single-row deep-groove ball bearing the factors depend on F<sub>a</sub>/C₀, the thrust compared with the static rating. If F<sub>a</sub>/F<sub>r</sub> ≤ e, then X = 1 and Y = 0, so P = F<sub>r</sub>. If F<sub>a</sub>/F<sub>r</sub> > e, then X = 0.56 and Y comes from the table below (the values printed in the standard and in most catalogues; interpolate between rows).

Because F<sub>a</sub>/C₀ needs the C₀ of a bearing not yet chosen, selection is a short loop: assume a bearing, read its C₀, find e and Y, compute P and C<sub>req</sub>, and accept the bearing if its C is at least C<sub>req</sub>.

sections.h3: Static check, speed check, and the order of work

blocks.text: A bearing that turns very slowly, stands still, or takes a heavy shock can fail with no fatigue at all. The rolling elements press dents into the race, called brinelling, and the bearing runs rough for the rest of its life. Against this the catalogue gives a basic static load rating C₀, the load at which a fixed small permanent deformation appears.
P₀ = 0.6 Fr + 0.5 Fa, but never less than Fr
P₀ is the equivalent static load in N for a deep-groove ball bearing; other types have their own factors in the catalogue.

The static safety factor is s₀ = C₀ ÷ P₀. Use about 1.5 to 2 for smooth, quiet running, 2 to 3 for ordinary machinery, and 3 or more where shock is expected. Every catalogue entry also carries a limiting speed, lower for grease and higher for oil; running above it heats the bearing faster than the housing can shed heat.

items: Find F<sub>r</sub> and F<sub>a</sub> on the bearing from the shaft loads (shaft design gives the reactions).
Fix the required life L<sub>10h</sub> and convert it to L₁₀ in million revolutions.
Assume a trial bearing of the right bore and read its C and C₀.
Find F<sub>a</sub>/C₀, then e and Y from the table; compute P = X F<sub>r</sub> + Y F<sub>a</sub>.
Compute C<sub>req</sub> = P L₁₀<sup>1/p</sup> and compare with C; move up a size if C is too small.
Check C₀/P₀ against the static safety factor, and check the limiting speed.

spec.aria: A deep-groove ball bearing with a radial load of 5 kilonewtons and an axial load of 2 kilonewtons, beside four boxes: life 720 million revolutions, equivalent load 6134 newtons, required rating 54 980 newtons, static factor 6.3.

examples.question: A deep-groove ball bearing of 45 mm bore carries F<sub>r</sub> = 5 kN and F<sub>a</sub> = 2 kN at 1200 rev/min and must give L<sub>10h</sub> = 10 000 h in ordinary machinery (s₀ = 2). Two bearings of that bore are available: A with C = 33.2 kN, C₀ = 21.6 kN, and B with C = 55.3 kN, C₀ = 31.5 kN. Select the bearing.
steps: Life in million revolutions: L₁₀ = 60 × 1200 × 10 000/10⁶ = 720. For a ball bearing L₁₀<sup>1/3</sup> = 720<sup>1/3</sup> = 8.963.
Try A: F<sub>a</sub>/C₀ = 2/21.6 = 0.0926, between the rows 0.084 and 0.11, so e = 0.287 and Y = 1.517. F<sub>a</sub>/F<sub>r</sub> = 0.4 > e.
Life check for B: L₁₀ = (55 300/6134)³ = 9.015³ = 732.6 million revolutions = 732.6 × 10⁶/72 000 = 10 175 h ≥ 10 000 h.
Static check: 0.6 × 5000 + 0.5 × 2000 = 4000 N is less than F<sub>r</sub>, so P₀ = 5000 N, and s₀ = 31.5/5 = 6.3 ≥ 2. Finally confirm that the catalogue limiting speed of B is above 1200 rev/min.
examples.answer: Bearing B: P = 6134 N, C<sub>req</sub> ≈ 55.0 kN against C = 55.3 kN, life ≈ 10 175 h and s₀ = 6.3.

traps: Putting L<sub>10h</sub> straight into C = P L<sup>1/3</sup>. The life inside the rating is in million revolutions, so 10 000 h at 1200 rev/min becomes 720, not 10 000.
Using Y when F<sub>a</sub>/F<sub>r</sub> ≤ e. Below the threshold Y = 0 and X = 1, so the axial load drops out; adding Y F<sub>a</sub> anyway inflates P and over-sizes the bearing.
Reading e and Y for one bearing and then choosing another. F<sub>a</sub>/C₀ changes with the bearing, so recompute P for the bearing you finally pick.
Skipping the static check. A shock-loaded or slowly turning bearing can brinell its races even when C ≥ C<sub>req</sub>.
Taking p = 3 for a roller bearing. It is 10/3, and the same P and L₁₀ then give a smaller C<sub>req</sub> than a ball bearing would.

quiz.q: What does the basic dynamic load rating C of a bearing mean?
quiz.a: The steady load in newtons that gives a rating life of one million revolutions; the catalogue lists it for every bearing.

quiz.q: State the equivalent static load for a radial ball bearing carrying thrust.
quiz.a: P0 is the greater of F<sub>r</sub> and 0.6 F<sub>r</sub> + 0.5 F<sub>a</sub>.

quiz.q: Why must L<sub>10h</sub> be converted to million revolutions before C<sub>req</sub> is computed?
quiz.a: C is defined for a life of one million revolutions, so the life in the rating equation must be in that unit. Using 10 000 h in place of 720 million revolutions gives 10 000<sup>1/3</sup> ≈ 21.5 instead of 8.96, so C<sub>req</sub> comes out about 2.4 times too large and the bearing is badly over-sized.

quiz.q: Why does the axial load stop mattering below the ratio e?
quiz.a: Below e the thrust is small compared with the bearing's static capacity, the load zone hardly changes, and life is set by the radial load alone. So Y = 0 and P = F<sub>r</sub>.

quiz.q: A ball bearing carries F<sub>r</sub> = 4 kN and no thrust at n = 900 rev/min, with a required life of 20 000 h. Find C<sub>req</sub>.
A roller bearing has P = 6 kN and a required life of 500 million revolutions. Find C<sub>req</sub>.
A bearing chosen on the dynamic rating fails within weeks, and its races show brinelling. What was missed?
quiz.a: The static check. Slow, stationary or shock loading dents the races even when C ≥ C<sub>req</sub>, so C₀/P0 must reach the static safety factor. The limiting speed, misalignment and fits are the other suspects.

beyond: Not for the exam. Standard L₁₀ gives 90% reliability; for higher reliability an adjustment factor a₁ below 1 multiplies the life, so the same bearing must be bigger. Modified rating life standards go further and correct C for oil film thickness, contamination and the fatigue load limit of the steel. In industry, bearing firms offer selection software and vibration-based condition monitoring that replaces a fixed life estimate with measured wear. Search for modified rating life, reliability adjustment factor, and bearing vibration signature analysis.
